lesson.title: Attention, Retention, Reproduction, Motivation: The Four Gears of Learning by Watching
lesson.summary: Observational learning is the specific process behind social learning theory, and Bandura broke it down into four component processes that all have to work for watching to turn into doing.
lesson.body:
Social learning theory establishes that people can learn by watching others. Observational learning is the name for that specific process, the mechanism by which watching a model translates into new behavior or knowledge in the observer. Bandura proposed that this process depends on four component steps, and if any one of them breaks down, the learning either doesn't happen or doesn't show up in behavior.

The first is attention: the observer has to actually notice and focus on the model and the relevant behavior. We don't learn from things we don't attend to, and factors like how interesting, similar, or high-status a model seems affect how much attention they get. The second is retention: the observer has to encode and store some mental representation of what was observed, since otherwise there's nothing left to draw on later. The third is reproduction: the observer has to be physically and cognitively capable of actually performing the behavior. A young child might attend to and remember a gymnast's routine perfectly but simply lack the strength and coordination to reproduce it. The fourth is motivation: the observer needs a reason to perform the behavior, whether that's an expectation of reward, a wish to avoid an observed punishment, or simple imitation of someone they admire.

This four-step breakdown explains a lot of everyday learning that has nothing to do with formal instruction. Children pick up their parents' speech patterns, expressions, and habits largely through observation. Apprentices learn a trade partly by watching a master perform it long before they're allowed to try it themselves. And in the internet era, people learn skills, styles, and even ways of talking from creators they will never meet, purely by attending to, remembering, and eventually reproducing what they've watched.

The clearest and most famous experimental demonstration of observational learning, showing that children will reproduce a behavior they've merely watched, with no direct reinforcement of their own, comes from Bandura's Bobo doll study, which is the focus of the next chapter.
